messages.content:
Validate the following vignette.

Patient demographics:
  age: 39
  gender: Female
  ethnicity: Latin American
  relationship_status: In a relationship
  occupation: Detective
  trauma_type: Witnessed domestic violence (childhood)
  pcl5: 75

Patient-reported symptoms:
  Triggers: Olfactory (Sweat/Body): Sweat or body odour, Tactile (Touch): Physical touch, Shouting: Shouting
  Maladaptive Strategies: Self-Harm Distraction: I hurt myself physically to stop thinking about the event, Avoid All Feelings: avoid anything that could cause negative or positive feelings, Avoid Being Touched: Any form of physical contact with others
  Threat: Waking Alert: I wake during the night to check whether I am safe, Startle to Movement: Unexpected movement nearby causes me to react as if I am in danger, Safe Seat Seeking: I always choose where to sit based on how safe or protected I feel
  Memory: Grief on Recall: When I remember the event I feel overwhelming grief, Hard to Recall Deliberately: When I try to deliberately remember what happened I find it difficult to access the memory, Visual Memories: My memories of the frightening event are mostly pictures or images.
  Negative Appraisals: Fear Going Crazy: My reactions since the event mean that I am going crazy, Self-Doubt: I can't trust that I will do the right thing, Character Blame: The event happened to me because of the sort of person I am

Vignette:
Sofia remembers the smell first. It was the scent of her father coming home from a long day’s work – sweat and something metallic, clinging to his clothes. That smell was the overture. Then would come the shouting, his voice a percussive force in their small apartment, ricocheting off the walls. She learned to make herself small, to disappear into the floral pattern of the sofa. The memories don't exist as a story she can tell; they come in silent, searing flashes. A close-up of her mother’s bruised cheekbone. Her father's hand, fingers curled into a tight fist. A glass of spilt milk spreading like a ghost across the linoleum floor. When she tries to deliberately summon the past, to line up the facts as she would for a case file, the details slip away, leaving only a hollow, overwhelming grief that settles in her chest.

Now, at thirty-nine, Sofia is a detective, a career she chose because she wanted to impose order on a world that had always felt chaotic. But the chaos followed her into the precinct. During a recent interrogation, a suspect, agitated and sweating under the hot lights, began to yell. The smell, the sound—it was enough. Sofia felt the room tilt, the air thinning until she couldn't breathe. The suspect’s face blurred and was replaced by the image of her father’s, contorted in rage. She had to excuse herself, her heart hammering against her ribs, convinced her partner saw her not as a competent officer, but as a fraud about to shatter. This deep, gnawing self-doubt has become her constant companion; she questions every report she files, every judgment call she makes, certain that she can't trust herself to do the right thing.

Her life has become a series of strategic retreats. She always sits with her back to the wall in the briefing room, her eyes scanning the door, a habit so ingrained she no longer notices she’s doing it. An unexpected movement in her periphery—a colleague rounding the corner too quickly—sends a jolt of pure adrenaline through her, her body tensing for an impact that never comes. At home, her partner’s attempts at affection are minefields. A simple touch on her arm can make her flinch violently. She has watched the hurt and confusion cloud his face so many times that she has begun to preemptively pull away from any physical contact, creating a chasm between them. To manage the intensity of it all, Sofia has learned to turn the volume down on her entire emotional life. She avoids movies that might make her cry, songs that might make her feel nostalgic, and parties that might make her laugh. Feeling anything, good or bad, has come to feel too dangerous.

Some nights, the visual flashes are relentless. To stop them, to claw her way back to the present, she will press her fingernails deep into the soft skin of her forearm until the sharp, grounding pain eclipses the images in her mind. She wakes often, her body rigid with alarm, and performs a silent checklist: doors locked, windows secure, her partner breathing steadily beside her. Only then can the terror recede enough for her to lie back down. She carries a secret, terrifying belief that these reactions—the flinching, the intrusive images, the emotional void—are proof that she is going crazy. She looks at her colleagues, at her partner, at strangers on the street, and feels a profound and frightening difference, as if she is a damaged thing pretending to be whole. This belief, which has shadowed her since childhood, is that the violence happened because of some essential flaw within her, that she was the kind of person bad things happen to. It was the growing fear of losing her career, and the quiet loneliness of the space she kept between herself and her partner, that finally propelled her to seek help, terrified that she is beyond repair but desperate for the chance that she might not be.
